idiom_name: base class with underscore-named primitives (or a sandbox object of engine functions) and an overridden entry method
implementation_notes: JavaScript's class syntax gives the mechanics - extends, super and prototype dispatch - but the language has no protected visibility, so the primitive API is marked by convention: a leading underscore, the same convention Node documents for internal methods such as writable._write(), which is 'prefixed with an underscore because it is internal to the class that defines it'. Private #members are the opposite of what a sandbox needs, because they are invisible to subclasses (and therefore unusable as provided operations); Symbol-keyed methods are reachable by anyone holding the symbol, so they only obscure the API. What replaces the classic structure in much JavaScript code is passing a sandbox object - the engine handles and the few functions a behaviour may use - into a behaviour function or registering behaviours in a table, which also makes the primitive set trivially stubbable in tests. Keep the class form when behaviours share instance state and a registration lifecycle.
pitfalls: The underscore is documentation, not enforcement: any consumer can call obj._playSound(), and nothing warns when a subclass redefines a primitive, so the sandbox is only as good as the code review around it.

Extracted methods lose this - a primitive passed as a callback runs with undefined or a global receiver and throws on the private field access - so bind the primitive or hand out a sandbox object of bound functions.
A base-class constructor that calls the sandbox method runs before the subclass's own field initialisers, so the behaviour observes undefined fields.
Misusing #privates for the primitive API makes the pattern impossible: subclass code cannot reach the member at all, so behaviours are forced to re-implement it or to use the engine directly.
